{"chapter_id":"qa-empty-hub","body":"# Laozi — The Empty Hub
*Tao Te Ching, chapter 11, translated by James Legge (1891), Project Gutenberg eBook #216 (public domain in the USA) · ~4 minutes*

## In their own words
> The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends. Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends. The door and windows are cut out (from the walls) to form an apartment; but it is on the empty space (within), that its use depends. Therefore, what has a (positive) existence serves for profitable adaptation, and what has not that for (actual) usefulness. [1]

## The compression
**My compression: we make things out of material, but we use them through the gaps the material leaves. The solid part gives a thing its shape. The empty part is where the thing actually does its work.**

## How this mind moves
**It starts with objects anyone can picture.** The chapter doesn't open with a definition of emptiness. It opens with a cartwheel, a clay pot and a room. Each one is plainly made by someone: spokes are joined, clay "is fashioned," doors and windows "are cut out." So the argument rests on the experience of making and using things, not on speculation about the cosmos. It's hard to disagree with the examples. A pot with no hollow can't hold anything, and a hub filled solid can't take an axle. That's the strength of the passage: it gets the reader to agree before the abstract claim arrives.

**It keeps pointing away from what we notice.** Look at a wheel and you see thirty spokes and a rim, the parts that took skill to build. The text sends your attention to the one part nobody shaped: the hole for the axle. The same thing happens three times. Each sentence names the craftsmanship first, then turns on a "but" and moves the use somewhere else: "it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends" [1]. Repeating that turn three times is the argument. When the same pattern holds for a vehicle, a container and a building, it starts to look like a principle, not a lucky example.

**It gives both sides a job.** It would be easy to read the chapter as "emptiness good, matter bad." The last sentence rules that out. Whatever "has a (positive) existence serves for profitable adaptation," and what lacks it serves "for (actual) usefulness" [1]. The claim is about how being and non-being divide the labour: the walls make the room possible, and the space inside is what makes it a room. This is the strongest objection to a simple cult of emptiness, and the text itself states it. With no clay you have no hollow at all. Some caution is needed here. The bracketed words — "(positive)," "(actual)," "(within)" — appear to be words Legge added to make the compact original readable in English. So the exact balance between "profitable adaptation" and "usefulness" depends partly on how he read the text. The idea of shared roles is clearly there. The precise wording of each role is his interpretation.

**It describes before it advises.** Strictly speaking, the chapter makes no recommendation. It says what use depends on, not what anyone ought to do. Turning that into a rule for living, such as "protect the empty spaces," is a step the reader takes. That step is reasonable, but it goes beyond what the text says, and it's better to be clear that we're taking it.

## Why today
Look at a work calendar booked from nine to six with no gaps. Every block is filled, and each meeting was arranged with some care, like the spokes. But the work the meetings exist to support has nowhere to happen. The calendar is all structure and no hub. The same pattern shows up in a flat filled with furniture until no one can move around in it, or in a piece of software that keeps adding buttons until the screen has no room left for what the user came to do. Chapter 11 offers a test for these situations. When something stops working, don't only ask what is missing from it. Ask whether there is still an empty space in it for the use to happen. The final line also gives the other half of the test. Clearing everything out doesn't help, because without walls there is no room. What matters is whether the solid parts are holding a space open or filling it.

## Carry this question
In the thing you're building right now, which part is the hollow that does the work, and is anything you've added filling it in?

## Sources
[1] https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/216/pg216.txt — Laozi, *Tao Te Ching*, chapter 11, translated by James Legge (1891), Project Gutenberg eBook #216; public domain in the USA. All quotations come from this translation.
